reviewers.summary: The paper acknowledges important limitations but still presents same-hospital readmission/reintervention comparisons as primary results, which are likely severely biased due to incomplete follow-up. The lack of competing-risk analysis for nonfatal outcomes in this high-mortality population additionally weakens causal interpretation. Major revisions are needed to either remove or substantially qualify these outcomes, and provide appropriate sensitivity analyses or alternative methods.

findings.title: Same‑hospital readmission and reintervention outcomes are likely biased by differential loss to follow‑up
evidenceRefs: paper.md: one‑year outcomes tables, adjusted model findings for HF readmission, cardiac readmission, valve reintervention
findings.whyItMatters: Because MIMIC‑IV captures only events within the same hospital system, the absolute risk and hazard ratios for readmission and reintervention may be strongly biased if dialysis status influences the probability of being readmitted elsewhere. The paper admits this limitation but does not discuss its likely magnitude or direction, and still reports p‑values and ORs without explicit warning that those estimates could be artefacts of ascertainment bias. This undermines the interpretability of most non‑mortality outcomes.
findings.actionableFix: Either drop all readmission and reintervention comparisons from the main results, or perform a formal quantitative bias analysis (e.g., sensitivity analysis under assumed proportions of outside‑hospital events) and downgrade the interpretation to hypothesis‑generating only. If retained, the abstract and conclusion must prominently flag that readmission/reintervention HRs are uninterpretable because of incomplete follow‑up.

findings.title: Competing risks not accounted for in nonfatal time‑to‑event analyses
evidenceRefs: paper.md: event‑specific Cox models for HF readmission, cardiac readmission, valve reintervention; limitation statement 'Fine‑Gray competing‑risk models were not estimated'
findings.whyItMatters: Mortality is high in the dialysis group (e.g., 35% at one year). When death is a competing event, cause‑specific hazard ratios can overstate the effect on the cumulative incidence of readmission. The reported HRs may mislead readers about the clinical probability of readmission, especially for dialysis patients.
findings.actionableFix: Re‑analyse these endpoints using Fine‑Gray subdistribution hazard models, or supplement the cause‑specific Cox models with cumulative incidence curves and clearly explain that the HRs do not reflect cumulative incidence. At minimum, add a statement that cause‑specific HRs should not be interpreted as the effect on risk of readmission.

findings.title: Propensity‑score matched sensitivity analysis only presented for one‑year outcomes
evidenceRefs: paper.md: 'Propensity‑Score Sensitivity' section reports only death_1y and mace_1y
findings.whyItMatters: The main analysis includes five‑year outcomes, but the matched analysis, which is intended to strengthen causal inference, is restricted to one year. This limits the ability to assess whether the propensity‑score adjustment would alter long‑term comparisons.
findings.actionableFix: Extend the matched analysis to five‑year mortality and MACE using the same matching set or explain why longer follow‑up is not feasible (e.g., small numbers). If added, report risk differences and McNemar’s test results for five‑year endpoints.

findings.title: Dialysis group 'hemodialysis or unspecified dialysis' mixes known and uncertain modality
findings.whyItMatters: If some patients classified as 'unspecified' actually received peritoneal dialysis (e.g., if peritoneal‑specific CPT codes were missed or not recorded), the dialysis group may be heterogeneous. Given the very small peritoneal dialysis subgroup, misclassification could dilute the contrast with non‑dialysis patients.
findings.actionableFix: Report how many of the 167 patients had explicit hemodialysis codes vs only generic dialysis codes. If possible, perform a sensitivity analysis excluding the 'unspecified' subset, or at least discuss the potential impact on effect estimates.

findings.title: Run directory artifacts not provided for independent verification
evidenceRefs: paper.md: 'The run directory contains aggregate code‑match, cohort, outcome, model, propensity, figure, QA'
findings.whyItMatters: The manuscript refers to a 'reviewer‑ready MIMIC packet', but the actual CSV/JSON/PNG files and any accompanying code are absent from the review packet. Without them, the reviewer cannot confirm that phenotype definitions, cohort assembly, and statistical modeling steps were correctly implemented.
findings.actionableFix: Include the referenced run directory files as supplementary materials with the manuscript submission, or provide a stable repository link containing all aggregate outputs and the exact analysis code.

missingEvidence: Run directory artifacts (aggregate CSV files, outcome‑phenotype JSON, figures, QA outputs) and analysis code are not included in the review packet, which prevents verification of data processing steps, phenotype rules, and model building.

reviewers.summary: The ICD-9 procedure code list for SAVR is incomplete (only 35.21, 35.22), missing standard codes such as 35.23, 35.24. This likely misclassifies many SAVR patients, potentially invalidating all valve-strategy comparisons and dialysis-specific estimates. This must be resolved before the analysis can be considered credible. Other major issues include incomplete documentation of the ICD-10-PCS phenotype rule, possible under-ascertainment of valve reinterventions in ICD-9 era, and lack of competing-risk analysis for nonfatal outcomes.

findings.title: Incomplete ICD-9 SAVR procedure code list
evidenceRefs: The user-supplied SAVR ICD-9 procedure codes were 35.21 and 35.22.
findings.whyItMatters: Standard ICD-9 aortic valve replacement also includes 35.23 (bioprosthetic) and 35.24 (prosthetic), among others. Excluding these codes can lead to substantial misclassification of valve strategy, biasing all subsequent comparisons and making the cohort non‑representative of true SAVR patients.
findings.actionableFix: Expand the ICD-9 SAVR code list to all relevant codes (35.21–35.24, possibly 35.20 for endoscopic replacement) and validate against procedure text. Reconstruct the cohort and rerun all analyses.
findings.deterministicVerification: Check the MIMIC procedure tables for codes 35.23 and 35.24; if present, patients currently excluded should be reclassified.

findings.title: ICD-10-PCS valve phenotype rule not documented
evidenceRefs: ICD-10-PCS aortic-valve replacement classification was derived from code-axis/title logic and should be treated as a reviewed phenotype rule, not a raw exact-code list.
findings.whyItMatters: Without the actual rule or code list, the ICD-10‑PCS part of the cohort definition is not reproducible and cannot be independently validated.
findings.actionableFix: Provide the explicit logic (e.g., which axis values were used) or the final mapped ICD-10-PCS codes in an appendix/supplementary file.

findings.title: Valve reintervention phenotype missing ICD-9 revision codes
evidenceRefs: Valve reintervention combined later TAVR, later SAVR, and ICD-10-PCS title-based revision/explant proxy evidence.
findings.whyItMatters: MIMIC contains both ICD‑9 and ICD‑10 eras. Ignoring ICD‑9 revision/explant codes (e.g., 35.13, 35.23) underestimates reintervention rates and may bias comparisons, especially for earlier years where follow‑up is longer.
findings.actionableFix: Incorporate standard ICD‑9 procedure codes for aortic valve revision/replacement into the reintervention definition.
findings.deterministicVerification: Query MIMIC for ICD‑9 procedure codes that are clearly aortic valve revisions and compare counts with the current definition.

findings.title: Cox models for nonfatal outcomes ignore competing risks
evidenceRefs: Nonfatal readmission/reintervention Cox models censor deaths before nonfatal events; Fine-Gray competing-risk models were not estimated.
findings.whyItMatters: In this population, early death is a strong competing risk. Cause‑specific hazard ratios may be misleading if one does not recognise they are conditional on survival. Reported HR e.g. 0.95 for HF readmission in dialysis patients may be distorted.
findings.actionableFix: Either reframe the interpretation as cause‑specific HRs and stress the conditional interpretation, or supplement with subdistribution hazard models (Fine‑Gray) for the primary nonfatal outcomes.

findings.title: No quantification of bias from same-hospital-only outcomes
evidenceRefs: Same-hospital readmission and reintervention outcomes may miss outside-hospital events.
findings.whyItMatters: Differential loss to follow‑up (e.g., dialysis patients more likely to be readmitted elsewhere) could bias the estimated associations. The lack of any sensitivity analysis weakens the conclusions.
findings.actionableFix: Provide a sensitivity analysis bounding the potential impact, or at minimum a detailed discussion referencing external data on readmission patterns for these patient groups.

missingEvidence: valve-phenotype-code-list.csv and outcome-phenotypes.json not available for inspection; full ICD-10-PCS rule not documented.

reviewers.summary: The manuscript reports a comprehensive same-hospital analysis of dialysis status and AVR outcomes using MIMIC-IV, but key statistical reporting and reproducibility elements are absent or incomplete. Proportional hazards assumptions were not tested, propensity score matching details are insufficient, some models risk overfitting, and supporting phenotype/balance files are not available for verification. These issues prevent full confidence in the reported estimates and transparency.

findings.title: Cox proportional hazards assumption not assessed
evidenceRefs: Cox model results for death, HF readmission, cardiac readmission, MACE, valve reintervention
findings.whyItMatters: If the proportional hazards assumption is violated, hazard ratios are biased and their interpretation is invalid. Dialysis status and valve type may exhibit non-proportional effects over time, especially for mortality where risk likely varies with post-operative phase.
findings.actionableFix: Test each Cox model using scaled Schoenfeld residuals (global and per covariate). Report results. If violated, adopt time-dependent coefficients, landmark analyses, or restricted mean survival times. At minimum, graphically assess log-minus-log plots.
findings.deterministicVerification: Compute cox.zph(model) for each survival model and report p-values and plots.

findings.title: Incomplete reporting of propensity score matching
findings.whyItMatters: Readers cannot assess match quality without full balance diagnostics (standardized differences for all covariates before and after matching), clear description of matching ratio (1:1? with replacement?), number of controls used, exact caliper scale (logit of propensity), and whether greedy or optimal matching was performed.
findings.actionableFix: Provide a comprehensive balance table with pre- and post-matching standardized mean differences for every covariate, specify the matching ratio, whether matching was with replacement, the number of discarded treated subjects (only 1 untreated?), and confirm caliper definition. Include a Love plot (already referenced as Figure 4) with all covariates labeled.
findings.deterministicVerification: Check that for each covariate listed in propensity model, the SMD before and after appears in the paper or balance table.

findings.title: Potential overfitting in valve reintervention Cox model
findings.whyItMatters: With only 96 events and multiple adjustment variables (dialysis, valve strategy, age, sex, Charlson, insurance categories, anchor-year groups), the events-per-variable ratio may be too low (likely <10) to yield stable estimates. This increases the risk of spurious findings and unreliable confidence intervals.
findings.actionableFix: Either simplify the model (e.g., use Firth’s penalized likelihood for logistic, or reduce covariates) or explicitly state that this analysis is underpowered and should be interpreted with caution. Alternatively, Firth’s logistic or exact methods could be applied for rare events.
findings.deterministicVerification: Count the number of degrees of freedom in the valve reintervention Cox model and confirm the events-per-variable ratio is ≥10; if not, adjust model complexity.

findings.title: Key data artifacts not available in the review packet
findings.whyItMatters: Without these files, the exact phenotype definitions, code lists, balance statistics, and graphical summaries cannot be verified against the paper claims. The study's transparency and reproducibility are undermined.
findings.actionableFix: Include all referenced supporting files (at minimum the outcome phenotype JSON, valve code list CSV, propensity balance CSV, and the figures) in the final manuscript supplement or as an appendix. Ensure they exactly match the versions used in the analysis.
findings.deterministicVerification: Confirm that every file path referenced in the paper exists and matches its description; MD5 checksums could be provided.

findings.title: No discrimination or calibration reported for logistic models
findings.whyItMatters: While logistic regression is common, reporting only odds ratios and p-values without model fit statistics (e.g., C-statistic, Hosmer-Lemeshow test) obscures the predictive performance of the models. Poor calibration could bias odds ratios if the model is misspecified.
findings.actionableFix: Add C-statistics and calibration metrics (e.g., Brier score, Hosmer-Lemeshow test) for each logistic model. Mention if any variable exhibited collinearity (VIF).
findings.deterministicVerification: Compute and report C-statistic and Hosmer-Lemeshow p-value for each logistic outcome model.

missingEvidence: Complete model diagnostic outputs (proportional hazards tests, VIF, calibration plots)

reviewPanel.nextAction: Adjudicate findings and route accepted repairs back into the pipeline.
